Ports as Critical Infrastructure in a Digital Era

The maritime transport sector underpins international trade, with ports and shipping networks

carrying around 80 percent of global trade by volume (UNCTAD 2025). Beyond their role as

transport gateways, ports serve as vital nodes in supply chains, connecting producers to consumers

across continents, facilitating the movement of raw materials and finished goods, and supporting

economic development in countries at all income levels. Ports are especially important for economic

activity in low-income countries and small island developing states (SIDS); according to Verschuur

et al. (2022), low-income countries are about 1.5 times, and SIDS about 2 times, more dependent

on maritime trade than the global average. Owing to this central economic function and systemic

importance, ports are increasingly recognized as critical infrastructure (CI).

Box 3 Cybersecurity considerations within the ISPS Code

The ISPS Code is structured in two parts:

• Part A sets out mandatory requirements, including the obligation for port facilities to

conduct a Port Facility Security Assessment and to develop, implement, and maintain

an approved Port Facility Security Plan. The latter defines measures to prevent, detect,

and respond to security threats affecting port infrastructure, operations, personnel,

and cargo.

• Part B provides non-mandatory guidance on how to meet the requirements of Part A,

including illustrative examples of risks and mitigation measures.

Despite its broad governance scope, the ISPS Code was designed primarily to address

physical security risks and has undergone only limited updates since its adoption.

Cybersecurity is not included among the mandatory requirements in Part A. References

Effective governance is the cornerstone of port cybersecurity. International frameworks currently

provide mostly non-binding guidance, placing the burden of implementation on national authorities.

Many countries designate ports as critical infrastructure and have national cybersecurity

protection, reporting and response, and resilience and continuity. However, the effectiveness

of these frameworks ultimately depends on how they are translated into local governance

arrangements within ports, where responsibilities are assigned, oversight is exercised, and

Box 10 Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation overview

ROSI quantifies the economic value of a security control by estimating the avoided losses

relative to the control’s cost. It adapts the classic return-on-investment (ROI) approach to a

loss-prevention context, answering whether a given security expenditure is cost-effective.

Key inputs:

• Single Loss Expectancy (SLE): estimated monetary loss per incident (includes direct and

indirect impacts).

• Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO): expected frequency of incidents per year.

• Annual Loss Expectancy (ALE): SLE × ARO. This is the baseline risk exposure.

• Control efficacy (mitigation rate): proportion by which the control reduces ALE.

• Total cost of control: acquisition, implementation, operations.

Core calculation:

• ROSI = [(ALE × mitigation rate) – cost of control] / cost of control

Los Angeles Cyber Resilience Center
